hints: Focus on the clues for X, a solid contaminant in fossil fuels that forms an oxide on burning and causes acid rain.
Identify X as sulfur, so Y is $\text{SO}_2$ and Z is $\text{SO}_3$, then check the electron configuration of sulfur for statement 1.
Recall how $\text{SO}_2$ is oxidised in the air and what happens when $\text{SO}_3$ dissolves in rainwater to test statements 2 and 3.
walkthrough:
**Identify X, Y and Z**

Think like a detective. A solid contaminant of coal and oil that burns to give an acidic oxide is sulfur.

$$\text{S(s) + O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{SO}_2\text{(g)}$$ So $\text{X = S}$, $\text{Y = SO}_2$ and further oxidation gives $\text{Z = SO}_3$:
$$\text{2SO}_2\text{(g) + O}_2\text{(g)} \rightarrow \text{2SO}_3\text{(g)}$$

**Check statement 1 about p electrons**

Write the electron configuration of sulfur, atomic number 16.

$$\text{S: 1s}^2 \text{2s}^2 \text{2p}^6 \text{3s}^2 \text{3p}^4$$ The $\text{3p}^4$ subshell has three orbitals, so one orbital holds a pair and two hold single electrons. Atoms of X do have paired p electrons, so statement 1 is correct.

**Check statement 2 about catalysed oxidation**

In the atmosphere, $\text{SO}_2$ is oxidised to $\text{SO}_3$ very slowly on its own.

In polluted air this oxidation is catalysed by nitrogen oxides, dust particles and metal ions in droplets. So statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3 about strong acid formation**

$\text{SO}_3$ is the acid anhydride of sulfuric acid and reacts vigorously with water.

$$\text{SO}_3\text{(l) + H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4\text{(aq)}$$ $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ is a strong diprotic acid and a major cause of acid rain. So statement 3 is correct.

**Combine the conclusions**

All three statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct. That matches the combination for all correct.

options.A: Correct, because statements 1, 2 and 3 are all true. Sulfur has $\text{3p}^4$ with a paired pair, $\text{SO}_2$ to $\text{SO}_3$ oxidation in air is catalysed, and $\text{SO}_3$ gives strong $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ with water.
options.B: Incorrect. This option includes only statements 1 and 2. It wrongly leaves out statement 3, but $\text{SO}_3 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, a strong acid, so 3 is also correct.
options.C: Incorrect. This option includes only statements 2 and 3. It wrongly leaves out statement 1, but sulfur ($\text{1s}^2 \text{2s}^2 \text{2p}^6 \text{3s}^2 \text{3p}^4$) clearly contains paired p electrons.
options.D: Incorrect. This option includes only statement 1. It misses the atmospheric chemistry. Students choosing this may confuse sulfur chemistry with carbon ($\text{CO}$ to $\text{CO}_2$ giving weak carbonic acid), but here Z is $\text{SO}_3$ giving strong sulfuric acid via a catalysed oxidation.
